plan: Personal essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000018) about a summer at a bookbindery: series commas, appositive repair of a splice, parallel verbs, 'each of' agreement, nonessential 'which', double negative, contrast transition, fewer/less, an add-sentence relevance item and a redundancy item; plus the E017-02 resubmission with its defensible distractor replaced.

passages.title: The Shortcut
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, I took a job sweeping floors at Hanley & Daughters, a bookbindery that had operated on Water Street since 1934. The shop {{1|smelled of glue, leather, and old paper,}} and the radio on the workbench played the same baseball station all day. {{2|Mrs. Hanley was the owner, she}} had been binding books in that room for almost fifty years.

For the first few weeks, I only swept and watched. Mrs. Hanley folded large printed sheets into sections called signatures, sewed the signatures together along their spines, and {{3|then she glued}} each sewn block into a cover. Each of the hundreds of books on her shelves {{4|were}} sewn by hand. She never used the machine that sat in the corner, {{5|which she called "the shortcut."}}

In August, she finally let me bind a book of my own. My first attempt was a disaster. The stitches were uneven, the spine leaned to one side, and the cover {{6|wouldn't hardly}} close. I expected her to drop it in the scrap bin. {{7|Nevertheless,}} Mrs. Hanley studied it for a long time, turning it over in her hands, before she gave it back to me. "Now make one with {{8|less}} knots," she said.

I made eleven more books before school started again. {{9|}} Each one was a little better than the last. By the twelfth, the stitches were even, the spine was straight, and the cover closed {{10|flatly and evenly without any gaps.}} Mrs. Hanley put that book on the shelf beside her own, and it is still there today.

passages.title: The Millbrook Carousel
passages.text:
When the town of Millbrook bought its carousel in 1921, the ride {{1|costed}} more than the town's new fire truck. For decades it turned every summer in Riverside Park, its forty-two wooden horses carved by hand and {{2|it's}} brass poles polished each spring by volunteers. Children chose their favorite horses by name, and some families took the same horses year after year, as if they owned them.

By 1990, however, the carousel had fallen silent. Its motor {{3|had broke}}, several horses had cracked, and the town could not afford repairs. A plan to sell the horses to a collector was proposed twice and voted down twice. The horses were stored in a barn {{4|where they waited, unused and idle, for nearly twenty years without being used}}.

In 2009 a retired shop teacher named Walter Okafor offered to restore them. He had never carved a horse, {{5|but he}} had spent forty years teaching students to work with wood. {{6|Working in his garage, the horses were repaired by Okafor one at a time.}} He replaced missing ears and tails, filled cracks with matching wood, and {{7|repainting}} each horse in the colors shown in a 1925 photograph.

The work took six years, partly because Okafor insisted on using only wood from trees that had fallen naturally in the county. {{8|Okafor did not finish the job alone, though.}} Volunteers raised money for a new motor, and a local electrician rewired the ride without charge. {{9|In contrast,}} in the summer of 2015, the carousel reopened, and more than two thousand people lined up to ride it. {{10|Tickets cost two dollars, and the line stretched past the park's main gate.}}
passages.author: ai:claude

candidates.subskill: Commas in a series within a compound sentence
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: smelled of glue, leather, and, old paper,
choices.C: smelled of, glue, leather, and old paper,
choices.D: smelled, of glue, leather, and old paper,

candidates.evidence: smelled of glue, leather, and old paper, and the radio
candidates.explanation: The series is punctuated correctly, and the comma before "and the radio" joins two independent clauses.

B.rationale: No comma belongs between "and" and the final item of a series.

C.rationale: No comma belongs between a preposition and its object.

D.rationale: No comma belongs between a verb and the phrase that completes it.

hints: Does any comma separate words that belong together?

strategy.explanation: Remove commas that split a verb or preposition from what follows.

candidates.remember: Use commas between series items, not inside a phrase.

candidates.subskill: Comma splice fixed with an appositive
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: Mrs. Hanley, being the owner, she

candidates.evidence: had been binding books in that room for almost fifty years
candidates.explanation: Turning "was the owner" into the appositive "the owner," set off by commas, leaves one subject ("Mrs. Hanley") and one verb ("had been binding").

A.rationale: Two independent clauses are joined by only a comma, creating a comma splice.

C.rationale: "She" repeats the subject "Mrs. Hanley" and leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

D.rationale: The appositive "the owner" must be set off by commas on both sides.

hints: How many independent clauses does NO CHANGE create, and how are they joined?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate comma splices and doubled subjects.

candidates.remember: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Mrs. Hanley folded large printed sheets into sections called signatures, sewed the signatures together
candidates.explanation: The series is "folded …, sewed …, and glued …": three simple past verbs sharing the subject "Mrs. Hanley."

A.rationale: "Then she glued" breaks the parallel series "folded …, sewed …, and ___."

B.rationale: "Gluing" does not match the past-tense verbs "folded" and "sewed."

D.rationale: The past perfect does not match the simple past of the other verbs in the series.

hints: What form do the other verbs in the series take?
candidates.remember: Items in a series take the same form.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Each of the hundreds of books on her shelves
candidates.explanation: The subject is "Each," which takes a singular verb: "was." "Hundreds of books" is inside a prepositional phrase.

A.rationale: The subject is "Each," which is singular; "books" belongs to the prepositional phrase.

B.rationale: "Are" is plural and does not agree with "Each."

D.rationale: "Have" is plural and does not agree with "Each."

strategy.explanation: Cross out the prepositional phrase "of the hundreds of books."

candidates.remember: "Each" is singular, no matter what follows it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: She never used the machine that sat in the corner
candidates.explanation: The clause adds extra information about the machine, so a comma followed by "which" is correct.

B.rationale: "That" introduces an essential clause and is not used after a comma.

C.rationale: This creates a comma splice: two independent clauses joined by a comma.

D.rationale: No comma belongs between "which" and its verb.

hints: Is the clause extra information, set off by a comma?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for a comma splice or a misplaced comma.

candidates.remember: Use "which" after a comma; use "that" without one.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Hardly" and "barely" are already negative, so they should not be paired with "not": "would barely close."

B.rationale: "Wouldn't barely" is also a double negative.

C.rationale: "Would not hardly" is a double negative too.

hints: Which choices contain two negative words?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate every choice with "not" plus "hardly" or "barely."

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: I expected her to drop it in the scrap bin.
candidates.explanation: The narrator expected the book to be thrown away; instead Mrs. Hanley studied it carefully. That contrast calls for "Nevertheless."

B.rationale: Studying the book is not an example of the narrator's expectation.

C.rationale: Studying the book does not restate the expectation; it departs from it.

D.rationale: Mrs. Hanley's careful study is the opposite of what the narrator expected, not something similar.

hints: Does Mrs. Hanley do what the narrator expected?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship between sentences before choosing a transition.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: Knots can be counted, so the correct word is "fewer."

A.rationale: "Less" is used with things that cannot be counted; knots can be counted.

C.rationale: "Lesser" means smaller in importance, not smaller in number.

D.rationale: "The least" is a superlative and does not fit "make one with ___ knots."

candidates.remember: Fewer for things you count; less for amounts.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:

Bookbinding developed after the codex replaced the scroll, roughly two thousand years ago.

Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the narrator's first book was a disaster.
choices.B: Yes, because it gives historical background that the rest of the paragraph develops.
choices.C: No, because it shifts the focus from the narrator's progress to bookbinding's history.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the claim that Mrs. Hanley had bound books for fifty years.

candidates.evidence: Each one was a little better than the last.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph traces the narrator's improvement from the first book to the twelfth. A sentence about the ancient history of bookbinding interrupts that sequence.

A.rationale: The sentence says nothing about the narrator's book.

B.rationale: The rest of the paragraph describes the narrator's improving books, not history.

D.rationale: The sentence does not conflict with anything about Mrs. Hanley.

strategy.explanation: Decide the paragraph's focus before judging the addition.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: in a flat and even manner without gaps.
choices.C: flatly, evenly, and without any gaps.

candidates.evidence: the stitches were even, the spine was straight, and the cover closed
candidates.explanation: A cover that closes flat has no gaps. "Flat" says it once and matches the short items before it in the series.

A.rationale: "Flatly," "evenly" and "without any gaps" say the same thing three times.

B.rationale: This is still redundant and wordier than "flat."

C.rationale: This only adds commas to the same redundant list.

hints: Do the extra words add meaning?

strategy.explanation: Choose the shortest choice that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: When choices mean the same thing, the shortest is usually best.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: For decades it turned every summer in Riverside Park
candidates.explanation: The poles belong to the carousel, so the singular possessive "its" is correct.

A.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which does not fit before "brass poles."

D.rationale: "There" refers to a place and cannot show possession.

hints: Can you replace the word with "it is"?
candidates.revision_note: E017-02 resubmitted with choice D changed from "their" to "there": "their" could refer to the horses and was therefore defensible.
